Angle between the dish heading and the car\'s forward direction (about −177° when the dish faces backwards); used for the car heading on the Position page and by the inertial correction. Learned: measured while driving straight above about 22 km/h and kept up to date. Manual: your value is used from the start; the correction still replaces it on a drive that shows one more than 5° away. A change restarts the filter.

After 5 s without a dish position, apps get Android\'s own network position (cell towers and Wi-Fi) until the dish answers again. Coarse (tens of meters in towns, often hundreds on highways); needs Google Location Accuracy on.

The network fallback passes on Android\'s network location, which comes from Google\'s cell tower and Wi-Fi positioning and needs Google Location Accuracy on: Location → Location services → Google Location Accuracy. It is used only while the dish gives no position. Google may place the dish\'s moving Wi-Fi where it was seen before, so expect it to be coarse. With the fallback off, Google Location Accuracy is better off.
Inertial correction (phone motion sensors and dish heading)

Holds the car on its track when the dish position drifts off to the side of the road, and carries the position on from the motion sensors while the dish gives none, less accurate with every second (nothing is served once its accuracy passes about 300 m or its sideways uncertainty about 50 m, whichever comes first; on a winding road that can be within half a minute). Keep the phone in a fixed mount: it learns how the phone sits in the first minute of driving. Switch off to compare with the plain dish fix.
Off: Auto serves the dish fix moved forward by its age, as before, and nothing while the dish gives no position (the network fallback aside).

After 5 s without a dish position Android\'s own network position (cell towers, Wi-Fi) is let through and goes into the inertial correction as a weak input; it is used only when it is better than the dead reckoning. Needs Google Location Accuracy on.

The update is downloaded and installs when the dish restarts: at the planned time, or now. A restart takes a minute or two.

The dish restarts to install the waiting update. It is offline for a minute or two, with no position from it meanwhile: in Auto with the inertial correction the mock GPS carries on from the phone\'s motion sensors for a short while, less accurate every second, otherwise it stops at once (in Auto the network fallback may still pass on Android\'s network position). Azimuth is counted from north (0° = north, 90° = east); elevation 90° is straight up. The dish wants to sit level and face the sky; tilt means little while driving.

Saves what the dish and the router answer right now as one JSON file for support, and opens the share sheet. It only reads: nothing is changed. Wi-Fi passwords and keys are never in it, and neither is any position.

The middle is straight up; the edge is low over the horizon, north at the top. Gray is sky the dish has not seen.

In a moving car the map shows places the dish has been; it fills in over time and is best read when parked.

Share of each 45° wedge that is blocked; the north wedge covers 337.5° to 22.5°.
Erases the dish\'s picture of what blocks the sky; it starts again from nothing and learns from now on.
The dish forgets everything it learned about obstructions. The numbers here are incomplete until it has looked at the sky again, which takes a while. This cannot be undone.
Each command asks first and says what will happen. A control the dish does not implement, or refuses, is greyed out with its answer.
Restarts the dish. It comes back in a minute or two.

The dish restarts now and is offline for a minute or two, with no position from it meanwhile: in Auto with the inertial correction the mock GPS carries on from the phone\'s motion sensors for a short while, less accurate every second, otherwise it stops at once (in Auto the network fallback may still pass on Android\'s network position). A waiting software update is installed. The app notes this restart as sent from here.

A daily window in which the dish sleeps: no internet and no snow melting. Its Wi-Fi may go off too, and with it Star Nav\'s link to the dish (not yet checked on a Mini): look after the first night. Times are your phone\'s local time.
The length must be from 1 minute to 24 hours.
Every day from %1$s to %2$s (%3$s) the dish sleeps: no internet, no snow melting, and no position from it. The dish counts in UTC: the window starts at %4$s UTC and lasts %5$s minutes.
The sleep schedule is switched off; the dish stays awake all day.
How the dish heats itself to melt snow and ice.
The dish decides by itself when to heat.
The dish heats all the time. This uses much more power, which matters on a car\'s battery.
The dish never heats: snow and ice stay on it and can cut the signal.
When the dish may restart to install a software update, and whether it may put an update off for up to three days.
The hour must be from 0 to 23.
Allow putting an update off for 3 days

Which time zone the dish uses for this hour is not confirmed; the figure is shown as the dish reports it. A car dish that is off at night may never reach a 03:00 window: use Install now on the Overview then.
The dish will use these update settings. It does not restart now.
Lets apps on the Starlink Wi-Fi, such as this one, ask the dish for its position. Your Starlink plan can still refuse position requests.

The dish will answer position requests on the local network. It is not verified that a dish accepts this from a phone on its Wi-Fi: it may need the Starlink app, signed in, to turn it on once. The dish\'s answer is shown here.
The dish stops answering position requests on the local network: this app gets no position from it until you allow it again.
Switches off the dish\'s own satellite navigation receiver. It switches itself back on when the dish restarts. Useful to test whether the dish keeps a position without GNSS.
The dish stops using GNSS until it restarts. Its position may become less exact, stop, or come only from Starlink\'s own measurements: watch the Overview. This is a test; switch it back on when done.
Switches the dish\'s radio to the satellites off. Its Wi-Fi stays up, but there is no internet through it while the radio is off.
The dish stops talking to the satellites: no internet through it until you switch the radio on again. Position data may stop too.
The radio is switched on and the dish looks for satellites again.
This dish has no motors, so it cannot be stowed or unstowed.
Folds the dish flat or raises it again.
The dish moves to its stowed position and is offline until it is raised again.
The dish raises itself and looks for satellites.
Asks the dish to look for a new software version.
The dish looks for a new software version. A found update downloads in the background and waits for a restart; nothing restarts now.
Reset the dish to factory settings
Erases the dish\'s settings (sleep schedule, snow melt, update window, …) and restarts it.
All the dish\'s settings are erased and it restarts. It is offline for a minute or two: no position from it meanwhile. You may have to set it up again in the Starlink app. This cannot be undone.
A control stays gray from the dish\'s last answer. After a firmware update or an account change, forget the answers and try again.

The router was not probed: the phone is not on the Starlink Wi-Fi and no router address is typed under Connection.
Leave empty to use the Wi-Fi network\'s gateway. The router answers on port 9001 (gRPC-Web), then 9000.
Round trip of the router\'s own pings, and the share lost now and over the last 5 minutes. A dash means no answer.
Share of time the channel was busy. A high share from other networks means crowded air, which slows everything on that band.

Tap a device for details, to rename it or to pause it.
rx and tx are as the router sees them: rx is what the router receives from the device.
This is the phone you are holding. Pausing it would cut Star Nav off from the router and the dish, so it is not offered.
The name is stored in the router and shown in this list and in the Starlink app.
The router stops giving this device network access until you resume it. If this is the phone you are holding, the router cuts it off and Star Nav loses the router and the dish.
The router lets this device back onto the network.
The router reported no Wi-Fi networks.
The password is shown only while this screen is open, and Star Nav never stores or logs it.
The name of the router\'s network: one for both bands, or a different one for 2.4 and 5 GHz so a device can be told which band to use.
A Wi-Fi name is 1 to 32 bytes (a Cyrillic letter takes two).

The Wi-Fi name becomes: %1$s\n\nEvery device on this Wi-Fi, including this phone, is disconnected and has to join again under the new name, in Android\'s Wi-Fi settings. Until the phone is back, Star Nav has no dish and no router, and the position feed stops.
Sets a new password on every band of the router\'s network.
The network is open: anyone in range can join it.
%1$s to %2$s characters: Latin letters, digits, spaces and the symbols of an English keyboard layout (no Cyrillic letters, which Android cannot use in a Wi-Fi password).

The Wi-Fi password changes on every band. Every device on this Wi-Fi, including this phone, is disconnected and has to join again with the new password, in Android\'s Wi-Fi settings. Until the phone is back, Star Nav has no dish and no router. The password goes to the router and Star Nav does not store it.
A hidden network does not show its name in Wi-Fi lists; devices have to be given the name by hand.

The router stops announcing its Wi-Fi name. Devices that already know the network usually keep working, but some drop and need the name typed in by hand. If this phone drops, Star Nav loses the dish and the router.
The router announces its Wi-Fi name again, so it shows up in Wi-Fi lists.
A separate network for visitors, whose devices cannot see the others. Not every router accepts this from this app; the answer shows below.
The router creates a guest network on 2.4 and 5 GHz, protected by the password you give; its devices cannot see each other. The main network is not touched.
The guest network is removed and its devices are disconnected. The main network is not touched.

The change went through. This phone may now be off the Wi-Fi: join the network again, under its new name or with its new password, in Android\'s Wi-Fi settings. Star Nav then finds the router again by itself.

The change went through. The router may restart its Wi-Fi, so this phone may drop off it for a moment. If it does not come back by itself, join the network again in Android\'s Wi-Fi settings (a hidden network by typing its name). Star Nav then finds the router again by itself.
Bypass mode is on. The Mini\'s Wi-Fi is off, so this phone has lost the router and the dish, and Star Nav cannot reach them. Only the reset button on the Mini brings the Wi-Fi back.
Nothing was sent: the router\'s current Wi-Fi settings could not be read first, and a change has to start from them.
Nothing was sent: this change does not fit the router\'s current settings (for example, there is no such network).

Controls of the router. Each one asks first and says what will happen. Changes that can cut this phone off the router say so: the phone reaches the dish through the router\'s Wi-Fi, so Star Nav has no position feed while it is cut off.
Restarts the router built into the dish.

The router restarts. Its Wi-Fi is gone for a minute or two, so this phone loses the router and the dish, and Star Nav has no position until the Wi-Fi is back. The phone normally joins it again by itself.
Asks the router to look for new software now.
The router looks for a software update. If it finds one it may download it and restart itself later to install it, which takes its Wi-Fi away for a minute or two. The state shows under Status.
Which DNS servers the router gives to its devices. The filters use Cloudflare for Families: it blocks known malware sites, and optionally adult sites too.
IP addresses separated by commas or spaces, at most %1$s.
The router hands out these DNS servers: %1$s. Devices on its Wi-Fi briefly lose their connection while it applies them, and some keep the old servers until they reconnect.
The address of the router on its own network. Change it if it clashes with another network you connect to.

The router moves to %1$s. This phone leaves the Wi-Fi and has to join it again. Star Nav then finds the router at its new address by itself, unless you typed an address under Starlink > Connection: change that one too. Until the phone is back, Star Nav has no dish and no router.
The router measures the speed of the Starlink link.

The router moves data at full speed in both directions for about 10 seconds. On a fast link that is several hundred megabytes, and it counts against a limited or metered plan. The router runs the test against internet test servers, which see your connection; Star Nav asks it not to send the result to Starlink.
The test ended with an error.
Turns the Mini\'s own router off so another router can take over.

The Mini\'s Wi-Fi turns off. This phone loses the router and the dish, and Star Nav stops working: it needs the Mini\'s Wi-Fi. The Wi-Fi does not come back by itself and this app cannot bring it back. Only the reset button on the router does, and that resets the router\'s settings. You need another router on the dish\'s cable.
I understand that only the reset button on the router undoes this
The Mini\'s router starts again, with its Wi-Fi.
Wipes the router\'s settings: Wi-Fi name and password, paused devices, DNS, subnet and bypass mode.

The router goes back to factory settings and restarts: the Wi-Fi name returns to the default and the password is removed. This phone is disconnected and Star Nav loses the dish and the router until you join the network again. This cannot be undone.
Some controls are greyed out because the router said it does not do them for this app. After a firmware or account change you can let them be tried again.
The last 15 minutes of the router\'s own pings. A gap is a sample it could not take.
Pings lost to the satellite network, IPv4
Pings lost to the satellite network, IPv6

%1$s can hand every app on the phone a different location than the phone\'s own GPS receiver gives: the one from your Starlink dish, corrected with the phone\'s motion sensors. It works through Android\'s mock location feature, so navigation, maps and any other app that asks for the location get it.
Why: when the phone\'s GPS is jammed or spoofed, apps jump across the map or freeze. The dish has a position source of its own, so with the mock on apps follow the dish instead.
Switch the mock on to see what apps receive.
The location service is not running, so these values stay empty. They fill in while the mock GPS or a recording is on, or while the Position page is open.
Nothing is recorded, not even with the mock GPS on. Sessions already on the phone stay below: open, export or delete them. Switch logging on in Settings to record again.
Sessions are recorded when you start one on the Sessions page and, if you choose so there, whenever the mock GPS is on. They stay on the phone.
Off: nothing is recorded at all, not from the Sessions page, the notification or the mock GPS. A recording in progress ends now. Alerts, the mock GPS and the delivery check work as before.

How often the phone\'s accelerometer and gyroscope are read, for recordings and for the inertial correction. A change applies the next time the sensors start (a new recording or switching the mock on).
Free and open source software. The source code is in the project\'s repository, linked from the page you installed the app from.

No accounts, analytics, ads or crash reporting; nothing is sent to the developer. Recordings stay on the phone unless you export one. The app talks to your dish and router on the local network, and to map tile servers only after you pick a map background. \"Open in Google Maps\" hands the position to your maps app only when you tap it. Logging can be switched off completely above.

Using the GPS position ±%1$s m. It is not verified: there is no Starlink position to compare it with.
Using what apps get, the Starlink-based position ±%1$s m (the mock GPS is on).

Star Nav will open Starlink\'s own sign-in page inside this app. You sign in there with your Starlink account, once. Star Nav then uses that sign-in a single time to switch on \"location on the local network\" for your dish, and forgets it.

You type your password into Starlink\'s page, not into Star Nav: the app never receives it. The page runs inside this app, and an app that hosts a page could in principle read what is typed into it. Star Nav does not: it adds no script to the page and reads none of its fields, and its source code is public. If you would rather not, use the Starlink app instead.

This is the only time Star Nav talks to Starlink\'s servers, and only because you asked. It sends your sign-in cookies to starlink.com and one request that changes this dish\'s setting. The sign-in is kept in memory only and is deleted when this ends; nothing is saved on the phone.

Starlink publishes no interface for this. Star Nav uses the one Starlink\'s own website uses, so it may stop working at any time, and Starlink\'s terms may not allow other apps to use it. It is your own account and your own dish, and you use it at your own risk.
